summary: Describes extensions to the Simple Mode of Facsimile Using Internet Mail, adding features such as higher resolution, color, and confirmation of delivery and processing.

eli5.summary: Faxing by email can go beyond plain black and white. This adds sharper pictures, color and a way to confirm the fax arrived.

questions: how does email fax confirm delivery
what is the difference between dsn and mdn
how does a fax sender learn recipient capabilities
subtitle: Fax over ordinary email, with required delivery confirmation and optional higher-quality documents.

tldr.problem: The simple mode of Internet fax over email sends only a minimum image format and gives the sender little assurance that a fax was delivered or processed, unlike traditional fax.
tldr.mechanism: It requires senders to use Delivery Status Notifications for delivery confirmation and allows Message Disposition Notifications for processing confirmation, and it lets recipients advertise richer TIFF profiles that senders can then use.
tldr.outcome: Delivery confirmation is required and extra document features are optional, both built on existing mail standards. RFC 2532 is a Proposed Standard with no obsoleting or updating RFC listed.

today: RFC 2532 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends RFC 2305.

sections.title: What This Extends
sections.content:
RFC 2532 builds on RFC 2305, the simple mode of facsimile using Internet mail. It describes enhancements that can be combined into an extended mode of Internet fax. The goal is to work with existing mail transfer agents (MTAs) and mail user agents (MUAs) and to reuse standard mail features, rather than creating fax-specific ones that ordinary mail software is unlikely to implement.

Two features are standardized: delivery confirmation (required) and additional document features (optional). The wider goals are described in RFC 2542.

The RFC defines processing as rendering or transmitting a message's contents to a printer, display or fax machine, and processing confirmation as the recipient's indication that it can process the contents. A recipient is the device that does the processing, for example a mail client on a PC, a standalone device that fetches mail using POP3 or IMAP, or an SMTP server that prints incoming messages. Gateways between the telephone fax network and SMTP are not described, though they SHOULD behave like the senders and recipients defined here.
sections.eli5: This document adds two things to email-faxing: a receipt saying the fax arrived, and a way to send better pictures. It does so using email tools that already exist.

sections.title: Sender Requirements for Confirmation
sections.content:
Traditional fax acknowledges receipt and processing of every page. In Internet mail, delivery to the mailbox and processing (to paper or a screen) can be separated in time and place, so two standards-track mechanisms are used: Delivery Status Notifications (DSN, RFC 1891 and RFC 1894) for delivery, and Message Disposition Notifications (MDN, RFC 2298) for processing.

The sender's envelope-from address MUST be able to handle delivery failure messages. A sender that wants delivery confirmation MUST request a DSN by including the ESMTP keyword NOTIFY with the value SUCCESS. A sender that wants processing confirmation MUST request an MDN when it sends the message.

Because a recipient may silently ignore an MDN request at any time, MDNs MUST NOT be used for delivery confirmation, and a sender MUST NOT assume a recipient will answer an MDN request, even if it has before. The Disposition-Notification-To address MUST be able to receive MDNs, SHOULD also accept non-MDN replies from legacy systems, and SHOULD match the envelope-from address so responses can be automated.
sections.eli5: A sender can ask for two kinds of receipts: one saying the fax reached the mailbox, and one saying someone actually printed or viewed it. The second kind can be ignored, so it is only a bonus.

sections.title: Recipient and Infrastructure Requirements
sections.content:
Recipients SHOULD implement MDNs and SHOULD indicate supported media features in DSN and MDN messages as defined in RFC 2530. A recipient MUST be configurable to silently ignore an MDN request. An automated recipient not tied to a person MAY be configurable to always respond, but must always be configurable to never generate MDNs. A recipient MUST NOT send an unsolicited MDN to report success; it MAY send one to report failure, as long as an operator can always disable that.

A recipient that fetches mail with POP3 or IMAP MUST NOT generate a DSN, because the MTA already issued any requested notification when it put the message in the store. Such a recipient MUST NOT use the To, Cc, Bcc or other recipient header fields to decide the final mailbox or addressee.

The mail infrastructure must also help. The submission server used by the sender MUST support DSN, as must every mailer up to the one that talks to external mailers. On the receiving side, the Internet-accessible mailer and each mailer between it and the recipient MUST support DSN, and so MUST a recipient implemented as an SMTP server.
sections.eli5: The person receiving can choose to ignore requests for a 'someone looked at it' receipt. The mail system along the way must be able to give 'it arrived' receipts, and only the first mail stop should send them.

sections.title: Learning What a Recipient Can Handle
sections.content:
The simple mode allows only the minimum TIFF subset (profile S) unless the sender knows more about the recipient. Under RFC 2532 a recipient MAY support any of the TIFF profiles in RFC 2301 in addition to profile S, and SHOULD say so. A sender should recognize the feature tags defined in RFC 2531, whose matching rules (via RFC 2533) allow new features that older implementations do not know. A sender MAY send one message containing both the minimum TIFF and a higher quality TIFF using multipart/alternative.

Three ways to learn a recipient's abilities are described, and method 3 SHOULD be used: (1) the user configures it manually, (2) a directory such as LDAP or DNS holds it, and (3) it is returned in a DSN or MDN. A directory approach is only a future direction and is not defined here. The DSN/MDN approach needs no extra infrastructure and is automatic.

A sender MUST NOT send a message with no processable content just to provoke a capability response, since that would confuse a recipient not designed for it. A recipient SHOULD report its profiles and features even if it supports only profile S, so the sender can tell it complies with this specification. Senders that cache capabilities SHOULD provide a way to override the cache.
sections.eli5: Before sending a fancy color picture, you want to know the other side can show it. You can be told by hand, look it up in a phone-book-like directory (not defined yet), or learn it from the receipts they send back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 2305 apply here too. The new features add two more concerns.

Inaccurate capabilities. Wrong capability information could cause a denial of service. It can arise from a compromised or misconfigured directory server, a manual configuration mistake, compromised DNS or a spoofed MDN. A sender that caches capabilities SHOULD have a way to ignore or override the cached data.

Forged notifications. Forged DSNs or MDNs can give a sender incorrect information.
sections.eli5: If someone gives you the wrong note about what the other side can handle, your faxes might fail. A fake receipt can also trick you, so you should be able to throw old notes away.

sections.title: Notes for Implementers
sections.content:
If the usual submission server does not support DSN, the sender can implement mail routing as in RFC 974 and extra submission server functions from RFC 2476, so it is not limited by that server.

It is desirable for a sender to learn that a recipient could not process a message. If the recipient's MTA decides the message cannot be processed, it is strongly encouraged to reject it with status code 5.6.1 from RFC 1893, either in response to the end-of-mail-data indicator when enhanced error codes are supported, or afterward with a delivery failure DSN. The RFC notes this is better than using MDNs, because MDN requests may be ignored while MTA rejection happens whether or not the sender asks.

If the message has an MDN request and the recipient's MUA finds it cannot process the message, the MUA is strongly encouraged to answer, with disposition-type processed or displayed and disposition-modifier error or warning.
sections.eli5: The best time to say 'we cannot handle this' is as the mail first arrives, because that works even when the sender did not ask. If a person's program finds a problem later, it should say so in its reply.

viz.caption: THREE WAYS TO LEARN RECIPIENT CAPABILITIES

cells: Awkward and not automatic, but reflects current deployment.
A future direction through LDAP or DNS; not defined in this document.
Capabilities returned in DSN or MDN
SHOULD be used; no extra infrastructure and automatic.

items.title: DSN: delivery
items.text: Confirms delivery to the mailbox. Requested with NOTIFY=SUCCESS and issued by the mail system.

items.title: MDN: processing
items.text: Confirms disposition to paper or screen. The recipient may silently ignore the request.
